questions.prompt: In this capture, which IP address is the DNS server?
questions.explanation: The query goes TO 9.9.9.9 on port 53 and the answer comes back FROM 9.9.9.9.53 — that's the server (Quad9, as it happens). 192.168.1.50 is the client, using ephemeral source port 44123. The '+' after the query ID 21398 means recursion desired.

questions.prompt: What is this client asking for?
choices: The IPv6 address of chat.example.org
The IPv4 address of chat.example.org
The mail servers for example.org
A reverse lookup of 10.0.0.1
questions.explanation: 'AAAA?' is a query for an AAAA record — the IPv6 address. tcpdump prints the query type before the '?'. IPv4 would be 'A?', mail servers 'MX?', and reverse lookups appear as 'PTR?' queries for in-addr.arpa names.

questions.prompt: Reading the response line: what did the server tell the client?
questions.answer_display: NXDOMAIN — the name doesn't exist (note the 'exmaple.com' typo)
questions.explanation: tcpdump prints the RCODE after the query ID: 'NXDomain'. The 0/1/0 counts are answer/authority/additional — zero answers, one authority record (the SOA for negative caching). Look closely at the qname: the user typed 'exmaple.com'. Typos are the leading cause of NXDOMAIN in the wild.

questions.prompt: What's wrong here? Describe what this pattern of traffic indicates.
questions.answer_display: The server never responds — queries are retried and time out (server down, or packets dropped en route)
questions.explanation: Four identical queries, ~5s apart, retrying — and not a single response packet. The client (resolver) is timing out and retransmitting. Causes to chase: dead server, routing problem, or a firewall silently eating UDP/53 in one direction. Next step: test from elsewhere and check TCP/53 too.

questions.prompt: This client's DNS traffic looks different from plain old port-53 UDP. What protocol is in use?
questions.explanation: TCP to port 853 with a TLS ClientHello is DNS over TLS (RFC 7858). The queries themselves are invisible to the capture — that's the point. DoQ (RFC 9250) also uses 853 but over UDP/QUIC, and DoH hides in normal HTTPS on 443.

questions.prompt: One query, two answers. What attack does this capture show, and which response should you distrust?
questions.answer_display: DNS spoofing / cache-poisoning attempt — the FIRST response (198.51.100.66) is the likely forgery
questions.explanation: Two responses for one query ID means someone raced the real server. An off-path attacker who guesses the ID and port fires their forgery fast; the genuine answer arrives a beat later — but the resolver already accepted the first one. The suspiciously quick 4ms response with an unexpected IP is the fake. Defenses: source-port randomization, DNS cookies, 0x20 encoding, and DNSSEC.

questions.prompt: This is YOUR server (192.0.2.53) in the capture. What role is it unwittingly playing?
exhibit: ... thousands more, all to 198.51.100.9, from many query IDs ...
accept: open resolver being used for amplification
questions.answer_display: An open resolver being used as a DDoS amplifier/reflector — 36-byte queries trigger 3245-byte replies aimed at the spoofed victim 198.51.100.9
questions.explanation: Classic reflection/amplification: the attacker spoofs the victim's address (198.51.100.9) as the source, and your open resolver obligingly fires ~90x amplified ANY responses at them. Fixes: don't run an open recursive resolver, apply Response Rate Limiting, minimize ANY answers (RFC 8482), and beg your ISP for BCP 38 egress filtering.

questions.prompt: A workstation is generating a steady stream of queries like these. What is most likely happening?
exhibit: ... continuing at ~1 query/second, unique labels every time ...
questions.answer_display: DNS tunneling — data is being exfiltrated (or C2 traffic carried) in encoded query labels
questions.explanation: High-entropy base32/base64-looking labels, unique every query, steady cadence, TXT type, all under one domain the attacker controls: textbook DNS tunneling. The data rides OUT in the qname and IN via TXT answers, sailing through firewalls that trust DNS. Detection: label entropy, query volume per domain, and NXDOMAIN ratios. RPZ or an egress DNS filter can cut it off.

questions.prompt: Look at the case of the query name, and the case in the response. What technique is the resolver using?
questions.answer_display: DNS 0x20 encoding — random query-name capitalization as anti-spoofing entropy
questions.explanation: DNS matches names case-insensitively, but servers echo the question back byte-for-byte. Resolvers exploit this: randomize the 0x20 (case) bit of every letter and reject responses whose case doesn't match. An off-path spoofer must now guess the query ID, the source port, AND the exact capitalization. Cheap extra entropy, used by BIND, Unbound and Google Public DNS.

questions.prompt: 192.0.2.10 is the primary nameserver, 198.51.100.20 a secondary. Narrate what these four packets accomplish.
choices: The primary NOTIFYs the secondary of a zone change; the secondary checks the SOA serial, then pulls an incremental zone transfer
The secondary detects the primary is down and takes over as primary
An attacker is attempting an unauthorized full zone transfer
The primary is replicating its cache to the secondary
questions.explanation: This is the standard replication dance: DNS NOTIFY (opcode 4, RFC 1996) tells the secondary 'my zone changed'; the secondary ACKs, queries the SOA to compare serials, sees it's behind, and opens TCP for an IXFR (incremental transfer, RFC 1995) to fetch just the diff. Without NOTIFY, secondaries would only poll on the SOA refresh timer.

questions.prompt: What's wrong here? This resolver's outbound queries share a worrying pattern — what is it, and what does it enable?
accept: fixed source port and sequential query ids
predictable ids and port make spoofing easy
questions.answer_display: Fixed source port (53000) + sequential query IDs — trivially predictable, enabling off-path spoofing/cache poisoning (Kaminsky-style)
questions.explanation: Every query leaves from port 53000 and the IDs increment by one. An off-path attacker needs to guess ID+port to forge a response; here both are predictable, collapsing ~4 billion combinations to a handful. This is exactly what made the 2008 Kaminsky attack devastating. RFC 5452 mandates randomizing both; modern resolvers draw the port from tens of thousands of options and the ID randomly per query.

questions.prompt: These DNS-shaped packets aren't going to any DNS server. What protocol is this?
questions.answer_display: Multicast DNS (mDNS) — Bonjour/Avahi service discovery on the local network
questions.explanation: Port 5353 to the multicast address 224.0.0.251, .local names, query ID 0: that's mDNS (RFC 6762), here doing DNS-SD service discovery — a device asks 'any IPP printers around?' and the printer answers for itself. No server involved. Apple calls the stack Bonjour, Linux runs Avahi. It stays on the local link by design.

questions.prompt: This host has 'nameserver 10.0.0.2' and 'nameserver 10.0.0.3' in resolv.conf. Explain what the capture shows happening.
choices: The first nameserver is dead; after retries and ~10 seconds of timeout the stub resolver failed over to the second one, which answered
The client is load-balancing queries across both nameservers as designed
10.0.0.2 forwarded the query to 10.0.0.3, which answered directly
A spoofer on 10.0.0.3 answered a query meant for 10.0.0.2
questions.explanation: The stub resolver tries nameservers in resolv.conf order: two 5-second timeouts against 10.0.0.2, then failover to 10.0.0.3, which answers instantly. Every lookup on this box is eating ~10 seconds of latency — the classic symptom of a dead FIRST resolver, and why applications feel 'slow' rather than 'broken'. Fix 10.0.0.2 or reorder; 'options timeout:1 rotate' softens the pain.

questions.prompt: An unknown external host does this to your authoritative server. What are they attempting?
accept: trying to pull the whole zone
questions.answer_display: An unauthorized zone transfer (AXFR) attempt — reconnaissance trying to dump your entire zone; the server correctly Refused
questions.explanation: TCP to port 53 followed by 'AXFR? example.com' is someone asking for the complete zone — a standard recon move to map your infrastructure. The 'Refused' means the allow-transfer ACL did its job. Keep it that way: transfers only to known secondaries, ideally TSIG-authenticated, and consider alerting on refused AXFRs since they signal someone casing the zone.

questions.prompt: Your authoritative servers for example.com are melting under this. What attack is shown?
exhibit: ... 80,000 queries/second, every label unique, from millions of sources ...
questions.answer_display: A random-subdomain ("water torture" / PRSD) attack — unique junk labels defeat caching so every query hammers your authoritative servers
questions.explanation: Each qname is unique, so no resolver cache can absorb the load: every query for <random>.example.com punches through open resolvers and botnet clients straight to your authoritative servers, which drown answering NXDOMAIN. This is the attack that took down Dyn in 2016. Mitigations: overprovisioned anycast, rate limiting — and DNSSEC-signed zones let validating resolvers synthesize the NXDOMAINs themselves from cached NSEC ranges (RFC 8198), absorbing much of the flood.

questions.prompt: What is the COOKIE option doing in this exchange, and what attack does it frustrate?
choices: The client sends a random cookie, the server appends its own; future queries must echo it — proving the client's source address isn't spoofed
It tracks the user across queries for analytics, like an HTTP cookie
It caches the answer client-side so the query needn't be repeated
It negotiates an encryption key for subsequent queries
questions.explanation: DNS Cookies (RFC 7873): the client's random 8 bytes come back paired with a server cookie derived from the client's IP and a server secret. A follow-up query carrying a valid server cookie proves its source address is real — something an off-path spoofer can't fake. Servers can then rate-limit or refuse cookieless traffic during attacks, cheaply defanging spoofed-source floods and amplification. Like TSIG's little stateless cousin, with no keys to manage.

questions.prompt: 10.0.0.5 is the DHCP server. What is this packet doing?
choices: A dynamic DNS update (RFC 2136): the DHCP server registers the A record for a laptop that just got a lease
A zone transfer of example.internal to the DHCP server
A cache-poisoning attempt injecting a fake laptop record
The DHCP server asking which zone it should serve next
questions.explanation: Opcode 'update' with a Zone section naming example.internal and an Update section adding laptop-jsmith's A record: this is DHCP-driven DDNS. The lease fired, and the DHCP server (or the client itself, in AD environments) registered the name via RFC 2136; the PTR usually follows into the reverse zone. NoError = accepted. In production these should be TSIG/GSS-TSIG authenticated and limited by update ACLs — an open update policy is zone-hijacking-as-a-service.

questions.prompt: The query was for www.example.com — but look at what came back in the additional section. Why will a sane resolver discard part of this response?
accept: the additional record is out of bailiwick
cache poisoning via the additional section
unsolicited additional record for another domain
the server has no authority over bank.com
questions.answer_display: The additional record for login.bank.com is out-of-bailiwick — example.com's server has no authority over bank.com, so resolvers must ignore it (it's a cache-poisoning vector)
questions.explanation: This is the original cache-poisoning trick: stuff an unrelated record into the additional section and hope the resolver caches it. Bailiwick checking — standard since the late-90s BIND holes — says a server's response may only be trusted for names within the zone it was asked about, so login.bank.com from example.com's server goes in the bin (Unbound's 'harden-glue'). Any modern resolver caching that record is critically broken.

questions.prompt: What's risky about this response at the IP layer, and what modern practice makes it not happen?
accept: fragments can be dropped or spoofed
questions.answer_display: The 2372-byte UDP response got IP-fragmented; fragments are often dropped (blackholes) and are spoofable. Modern practice: advertise EDNS buffer 1232 so big answers set TC and use TCP instead
questions.explanation: The client advertised a 4096-byte EDNS buffer, so the server crammed a large DNSKEY answer into one UDP datagram that the IP layer split into two fragments. Trouble: many middleboxes drop fragments (silent timeouts), and the second fragment carries no UDP port or DNS ID — making fragment-injection spoofing practical (the 'first-fragment' attacks against DNSSEC key sets). DNS Flag Day 2020's answer: default buffer 1232 bytes; anything bigger truncates and rides TCP, which handles size honestly.
